finding_key: packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts::ssrf via unvalidated image `src` in the cli slides/docs export fetcher that this change promotes as a shipped feature
evidence: The code facts check out in the supplied files: `resolveImageUrl` in packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts explicitly passes through any scheme-bearing URL ("http:", "file:", etc.) untouched, and the returned fetcher does a bare `await fetchImpl(resolved)` with no scheme/host/private-IP allowlist; it is wired into `slides export` (packages/cli/src/commands/slides.ts, `createImageFetcher({serverBase: getConfig(opts).server})` → `exportPptxCli`) and both docs export paths (packages/cli/src/commands/docs.ts). The attacker-controlled-src premise also holds: `assertValidElement` in packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts validates only `id`/`type`/`frame`, never `data.src`, and packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts embeds whatever `fetchImage` returns verbatim as a `ppt/media/` part. So the described request-forgery/exfiltration mechanism is genuinely present as written. I rate it minor rather than higher because it is untouched pre-existing code (this diff only edits docs plus frontend/homepage files), the fetch originates from a user-run CLI rather than a network service, no credentials are attached, and exploitation needs deck write access plus a privileged runner plus access to the produced artifact; fetching remote image URLs is also inherent to the exporter's contract. My confidence is medium because I could not run the exploit chain or inspect `packages/cli/src/slides/pptx-export.ts` (not supplied) to confirm it forwards the fetcher unmodified.
